name: Fading affect bias
statement: The emotion attached to an unpleasant personal memory fades faster over time than the emotion attached to a pleasant one.
meaning: The bias is a difference between two difference scores. A person names an autobiographical event, rates how pleasant or unpleasant it felt at the time, and rates how it feels now. Subtracting one rating from the other gives the fading for that event. The fading affect bias is the finding that this drop is larger for unpleasant events than for pleasant ones. It is a claim about emotion rather than about recall. Walker and Skowronski's review says the founding studies found positive and negative events remembered with almost equal clarity while their emotions diverged. The 1997 abstract is weaker, reporting a modest memory advantage for pleasant events. Ritchie and colleagues split the outcome four ways in a 2009 study, which the same review describes: affect that stays fixed, fades, grows more intense, or flips valence. Only the second is fading in the literal sense, and the bias is a pattern across all four.

origin.who: W. Richard Walker, Rodney J. Vogl and Charles P. Thompson
origin.where: Applied Cognitive Psychology, volume 11, issue 5, pages 399-413
origin.note: Three diary studies in which participants recorded unique events and rated their pleasantness as they happened, then rated the same events again in the laboratory. Walker and Skowronski's 2009 review calls this paper the start of the modern era of the effect and names two earlier sightings it builds on, Cason in 1932 and Holmes in 1970. The 1997 full text was not obtained, so the design here comes from that review and from Walker, Skowronski and Thompson's 2003 account. Both give the retention intervals as 3.5 months, one year and 4.5 years, where the published abstract says 3 months, one year and 4.5 years.

evidence: Walker and Skowronski summarise the 1997 diary data as two trends: longer retention intervals produced more fading, and unpleasant affect faded more than pleasant affect at every interval. Their account of the sample is not self consistent, giving 38 participants at the 3.5-month interval in the text and 43 in the caption of the figure that plots it. Independent laboratories have since produced the same asymmetry with much larger samples. Marsh, Hammond and Crawford collected 2,368 memories from 296 students at Victoria University of Wellington, half positive and half negative, rated on a scale from -3 to +3 at occurrence and at recall. Positive affect faded less than negative affect, with a multilevel coefficient of -0.680 and a 95% interval from -0.743 to -0.617. Gibbons and four colleagues ran the same comparison on 284 in-person and 157 online participants at an American university. In the in-person study, with initial intensity held constant, the adjusted mean drop was 0.050 scale points for pleasant events against 2.001 for unpleasant ones, F(1, 2116) = 1048.833, p < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.331. The online study gave 0.416 against 2.243. Hoehne and Zimprich took 12,314 memories from 2,163 German-speaking adults aged 18 to 98. Scoring change from the rating difference, 39.7% of negative memories faded against 14.8% of positive ones. Scoring it from what participants said had happened to the memory, the figures were 30.5% and 10.3%. Ritchie and seven colleagues report the bias in each of 10 cultural samples, drawn from 2,439 events rated by 562 participants. The largest sample was 180 Germans and the smallest 14 Ghanaians, with African American, Caucasian American, Native American, New Zealand European, Maori and Pasifica, British, Black British and Irish samples between.

examples.text: A talk that fell apart stings for weeks and is told as a funny story a few years later. A talk that went well still gives a small lift when it comes to mind. Both are recalled clearly, and only the feelings have moved apart.

A day in horizontal rain on a hill is described afterwards as a good day out, with the cold no longer attached to it. A warm day on the same hill is remembered warmly still, which is the asymmetry the claim is about.

An argument that was unbearable at the time is retold at a family lunch without much heat left in it. For many memories the feeling does not shift at all in either direction, and the pattern shows up in the average rather than in every case.

replication.headline: The asymmetry turns up in every large sample that has looked for it, including all 10 samples of a pancultural study and independent laboratories in New Zealand, Germany and the United Kingdom, though its size varies with who is tested and one sample lost it under statistical control.
replication.detail: Marsh, Hammond and Crawford's study is the cleanest independent test with a published interval. Their multilevel model of 2,368 memories from 296 participants gives an unstandardised coefficient of -0.680 for the valence difference in fading, 95% interval -0.743 to -0.617, p < 0.001, on the study's own -3 to +3 rating scale. Hitchcock and six colleagues found the bias in both of the groups they tested at Cambridge. It gave d = 2.14 in the never-depressed group and d = 1.08 in 21 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder by structured interview. They recruited 23 never-depressed adults, but the fading test carries 21 degrees of freedom, so 22 were analysed. An analysis of covariance with age as the covariate put the gap between the groups at F(1, 40) = 6.97, p = 0.01, partial eta squared 0.15. Hoehne and Zimprich found it in 12,314 German-language memories by two different scoring methods. Ritchie and colleagues found the valence effect in all 10 of their samples, from F(1, 570) = 250.01 among African Americans down to F(1, 63) = 7.77 among Black Britons. Adding individual differences in event selection to the model left it standing everywhere but the Irish sample, where it fell to F(1, 292) = 0.00. Walker was an author of that paper and of the 1997 original, so it broadens the founding group's work rather than testing it from outside. Muir, Brown and Madill at Leeds found that disclosure to an unresponsive listener made unpleasant memories more intense rather than less, which moves the effect rather than removing it.

study.cite: Marsh, C., Hammond, M. D., & Crawford, M. T. (2019). Thinking about negative life events as a mediator between depression and fading affect bias. PLOS ONE, 14(1), e0211147.

limits: Depression is the documented boundary, and it is narrower than it is usually reported to be. Walker, Skowronski, Gibbons, Vogl and Thompson divided participants by Beck Depression Inventory score and titled their paper for the disruption. Their own conclusion is milder than the title: dysphorics showed a smaller bias, not none. The first experiment ran on 65 students at Kansas State, 19 dysphoric and 46 not, and the interaction came to F(1, 63) = 4.86, p < 0.05. The test inside the dysphoric group came to t(18) = 2.04, which missed a Bonferroni-corrected threshold, and that near miss is what later accounts repeat as a flat null. The second experiment pooled 337 students across three replications and sorted them into five dysphoria bands. The bias held in the lower four bands and failed only in the highest, F(1, 285) = 1.91. Two later studies with clinical measurement weaken the claim further. Hitchcock and colleagues found the bias attenuated but present in diagnosed major depression. Marsh, Hammond and Crawford found that higher Beck scores predicted less fading of affect overall, coefficient -0.010 with a 95% interval from -0.016 to -0.004. The interaction with memory valence, which is the bias itself, was flat. It came to 0.001, with an interval from -0.006 to 0.008 and p = 0.722. Anxiety is less settled. Walker, Yancu and Skowronski report anxiety by valence interactions in three samples of 98, 50 and 25 participants, so anxiety shrinks the bias itself and not only the fading. Their anxiety main effect held in the first two samples and failed in the third, F(1, 12) = 1.19, p = 0.27. Marsh, Hammond and Crawford found no anxiety effect at all in their 296 participants, on either fading or the bias, and say so against prior evidence. Method is a live worry. Most studies ask for the original emotion at the moment of recall, so both ratings come from one sitting, and Walker and Skowronski name retrospective bias as the standing criticism that the diary studies were run to answer. Two documents could not be had. Wiley answers a request for the 1997 paper with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall, and Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC and the authors' own pages listed no open copy on 21 September 2026. Its abstract was read from a 2015 capture of the publisher's record in the Wayback Machine. Holmes's 1970 paper is closed on the same terms, with the American Psychological Association's site answering an automated request with a bot challenge. Gibbons and colleagues' report of their own initial-intensity means contradicts the sentence describing them, so only their fading results are quoted.
misreadings: The fading affect bias and rosy retrospection, no. 81, are separate claims with separate evidence, and quoting one for the other is the commonest error. Rosy retrospection compares three evaluations of a single event, taken before it, during it and after it, and needs momentary ratings collected in the field. The fading affect bias compares the intensity of emotion at an event with the intensity of emotion at recall, across pleasant and unpleasant events, and needs no field measurement at all. One asks whether a holiday is remembered as better than it felt. The other asks whether the sting leaves faster than the glow. The second error is the flat statement that depressed people show no fading affect bias. The 2003 study behind it concludes that dysphorics show a smaller bias, not an absent one, and its dysphoric group was 19 students sorted by a questionnaire cutoff. Hitchcock and colleagues, testing people diagnosed by structured interview, found the bias reduced by roughly half and still reliable at d = 1.08. Third, the bias is often read as a claim that most memories soften. Hoehne and Zimprich found fixed affect the commonest outcome for both valences under both of their scorings, with 62.0% of positive and 47.9% of negative memories reported as unchanged. Fourth, people's own beliefs about the process run the other way. Crawford and Marsh asked participants to predict how affect fades. They expected positive events to fade more in the short term and negative events to fade more in the long term. That is not the pattern the data show.

sources.text: Walker, W. R., Vogl, R. J., & Thompson, C. P. (1997). Autobiographical memory: unpleasantness fades faster than pleasantness over time. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 11(5), 399-413. The founding paper. Citation verified at Crossref. The full text was not obtained: Wiley returns a Cloudflare bot challenge, not a paywall, and no open copy was listed anywhere searched on 21 September 2026. The abstract was read from a 2015 Wayback capture of the Wiley record, and nothing else is quoted from it.

Walker, W. R., & Skowronski, J. J. (2009). The fading affect bias: but what the hell is it for? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 23(8), 1122-1136. Read in full from the second author's posted copy. The source for the 1997 design and sample, for Cason and Holmes as antecedents, and for the 2003 dysphoria results.

Walker, W. R., Skowronski, J. J., & Thompson, C. P. (2003). Life is pleasant, and memory helps to keep it that way! Review of General Psychology, 7(2), 203-210. Read in full from a Wayback capture of the publisher's free release copy, which now answers with a bot challenge. A second account of the 1997 design by two of its authors.

Holmes, D. S. (1970). Differential change in affective intensity and the forgetting of unpleasant personal experiences. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 15(3), 234-239. Citation verified at Crossref; the review's own reference list gives the volume as 3, which is wrong. The full text was not obtained: the publisher's site answers an automated request with a bot challenge, and no open copy is indexed. Its finding is quoted from Walker and Skowronski's review.

Walker, W. R., Skowronski, J. J., Gibbons, J. A., Vogl, R. J., & Thompson, C. P. (2003). On the emotions that accompany autobiographical memories: dysphoria disrupts the fading affect bias. Cognition & Emotion, 17(5), 703-723. Read in full from the second author's posted copy, in the same directory as the 2009 review. An earlier note here called it unobtained.

Ritchie, T. D., Batteson, T. J., Bohn, A., Crawford, M. T., Ferguson, G. V., Schrauf, R. W., Vogl, R. J., & Walker, W. R. (2015). A pancultural perspective on the fading affect bias in autobiographical memory. Memory, 23(2), 278-290. Read in full from the author's accepted manuscript in Aarhus University's Pure repository, which served it to a plain request. An earlier note here called that copy blocked. The manuscript is not the version of record, so page numbers and wording may differ.
Marsh, C., Hammond, M. D., & Crawford, M. T. (2019). Thinking about negative life events as a mediator between depression and fading affect bias. PLOS ONE, 14(1), e0211147. Read in full.

Hitchcock, C., Newby, J., Timm, E., Howard, R. M., Golden, A.-M. J., Kuyken, W., & Dalgleish, T. (2020). Memory category fluency, memory specificity, and the fading affect bias for positive and negative autobiographical events: performance on a good day-bad day task in healthy and depressed individuals. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 149(1), 198-206. Read in full from the PubMed Central copy, which needs a browser-like user agent; a plain one draws a reCAPTCHA.

Gibbons, J. A., Vandevender, S., Langhorne, K., Peterson, E., & Buchanan, C. (2024). In-person and online studies examining the influence of problem solving on the fading affect bias. Behavioral Sciences, 14(9), 806. Read in full from Europe PMC's full text route.

Hoehne, S., & Zimprich, D. (2025). Evidence for a fading affect bias in subjectively assessed affect changes in autobiographical memory. Frontiers in Psychology, 16, 1608751. Read in full from Europe PMC's full text route; the four outcome shares come from its Table 2.

Walker, W. R., Yancu, C. N., & Skowronski, J. J. (2014). Trait anxiety reduces affective fading for both positive and negative autobiographical memories. Advances in Cognitive Psychology, 10(3), 81-89. Read in full from Europe PMC's full text route. The Crossref record lists only the first two authors; the published text names three.

Muir, K., Brown, C., & Madill, A. (2015). The fading affect bias: effects of social disclosure to an interactive versus non-responsive listener. Memory, 23(6), 829-847. Read in full from the author's accepted manuscript in White Rose Research Online at Leeds. Bath's copy of the same manuscript sits behind a Cloudflare challenge. The manuscript is not the version of record.

Crawford, M. T., & Marsh, C. (2023). Time heals all wounds? Naive theories about the fading of affect associated with autobiographical events. Memory & Cognition, 51(8), 1715-1728. Read in full from Europe PMC's full text route.

Marsh, C., & Crawford, M. T. (2024). Age is positively associated with fading affect bias: a cross-sectional comparison. Psychology and Aging, 39(2), 139-152. Read at abstract level only, from the publisher's own record at Ovid; two age-diverse community samples in which participants of all ages showed the bias and its strength rose with age. No open copy is indexed, and the American Psychological Association's site answers an automated request with a bot challenge.
